Yes — to be clear about the two sub-questions:

**PRs #8–#13** (the additive `packages/deploy-cloudflare/` work) live in your fork only. Upstream Paperclip wouldn't accept a Cloudflare-specific package; this is your deployment.

**PRs #1–#7** (the upstream seams: DB factory split, Scheduler interface, Handler shape, CommandExecutor, storage extension point, filesystem quarantine) — you have two choices:

1. **Land them in your fork only.** Faster. You own the seams, you own the merge conflicts when pulling upstream.
2. **Land in your fork, then PR each one upstream.** Slower (each PR needs review, tests, docs, justification *without* mentioning Cloudflare since upstream doesn't care about your deployment — pitch them as "improves testability"). But if any get merged, that's permanent surface area in upstream that your fork doesn't have to maintain.

The plan was written assuming option 2 because you said "abstracted so we can take advantage of all of the open-source updates." That goal is best served by upstreaming the seams: every seam upstream accepts is one less thing your fork has to rebase forever. But it's not required — option 1 still works, you just carry the seam patches in your fork as long-lived diffs.

**Practical recommendation**: do option 1 first (land in fork, ship Phase 1), then opportunistically upstream the cleanest seams (#1 DB factory split, #5 CommandExecutor) which are obviously-good independent of Cloudflare. Don't block your deployment on upstream review.

Either way, the *design* of those PRs as additive/non-breaking is what matters — it minimizes rebase pain whether they ever go upstream or not.
